new_statements.rule_in_words: Tangut (as reconstructed from the 12th-c. native rhyme dictionaries Wenhai/Tongyin and Tibetan transcriptions) is a tone language with a binary lexical tone opposition on every syllable (tone 1 平 vs tone 2 上; Beaudouin: high vs low; Gong Hwang-cherng: high-level vs rising). No modern description says anything about word stress or accent placement; the language is extinct and its prosody beyond tone class is not recoverable from the sources.
new_statements.exceptions: Beaudouin notes tone sandhi is 'inaccessible'; Hamada 2024 fn.4 cautions that the two-tone analysis is a working hypothesis inherited from the native philology; Nie (1997) proposed up to four tones (rejected by Beaudouin p.210 fn.14). Only 'accent' remarks found anywhere: Laufer 1916 pp.23-24 (speculative, diachronic, one etymology) and Miyake 2012 on pre-Tangut 'compression' (not opened).
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable/morpheme-level tone categories from rhyme dictionaries (citation forms of single characters); no word- or phrase-level prosodic description exists.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the single literary Tangut (Xixia, Mi-nyag) language of the 12th-c. rhyme dictionaries, glottocode tang1334 / ISO txg; no dialect issue. The language is extinct and known only through its script plus Tibetan/Chinese transcriptions, so any prosodic statement is a reconstruction.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tangut is described as a two-tone language (tone 1 = high, tone 2 = low, a syllable-level opposition reconstructed from the rime dictionaries and Horpa/Tibetan correspondences); the thesis contains no statement about word stress, accent or prominence at all. A full-text search of all 814 pages for accent/stress/proéminence/tonique/atone/intensité yields no phonological hit: 'accent' occurs only as 'mettre l'accent sur' (discourse emphasis, pp.474, 575, 655) and in a bibliography entry on Pattani Malay (p.793); 'intensité' is Gong's vowel 'tenseness' (sec. 9.3), not stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. The author notes tone sandhi is 'inaccessible' (p. xvi) and mentions one possible case of tonal sandhi in a lexicalised compound (p.496, p.547); footnote 11 p.208 reports Miyake (2012) doubting that the tones were originally contour tones at all.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes the written Tangut (Xixia) language of the 11th-13th c. texts (Leilin etc.) using Gong Hwang-cherng's reconstruction, with a revised reconstruction proposed in chs. 8-9; no dialect is distinguished. Because the language is extinct and known only through rime dictionaries and transcriptions, word stress is in principle unrecoverable from the sources, which is why the phonology treats only syllable-level oppositions (tone, grade, length/gemination, rhotacisation, tenseness).

tone_statements.quote: なお、西夏語音韻学では平声に第 1 韻から第 97 韻の、上声に第 1 韻から第 86 韻の韻目をそれぞれ設ける。例えば平声第 14 韻と上声第 12 韻は相配の関係にある（調類の違いで互いに対立する韻目同士である）。... 『文海』は本体部分と雑類にまず大別されており、本体部分は掲載字の声調に従って巻第一と巻第二に分けられ、そして雑類もまた掲載字の声調に従って、平声字を掲載する前半と、非平声字4（典型的には上声字）を掲載する後半に二分される。... 龔氏案の推定音は khu²（上付きの数字は調類（1 は平声、2 は上声）を指す）である。
tone_statements.translation: In Tangut phonology [the native Xixia science], rhymes 1-97 are set up in the level tone (平声) and rhymes 1-86 in the rising tone (上声). For example level-tone rhyme 14 and rising-tone rhyme 12 stand in a matching relation (they are rhymes opposed to each other by the difference of tone class). ... The Wenhai is first divided into a main part and the 'zalei'; the main part is divided into volume 1 and volume 2 according to the tone of the listed characters, and the zalei too is divided by the tone of the listed characters into a first half listing level-tone characters and a second half listing non-level-tone characters (typically rising-tone characters). ... The reconstruction in Gong's system is khu² (the superscript number indicates the tone class: 1 = level tone, 2 = rising tone).
tone_statements.summary: Philological paper: two tone classes 平声/上声 from the native rhyme books, pitch values not given; fn.4 p.22: a very few 入声 characters, status unclear. forms_shown = 14 tone-classed chars + khu².

tone_statements.quote: Tangut tones are a more complex issue than what is presented here. tone_statements.quote: The phonetic transcriptions in Tibetan scripts are also discussed from the viewpoint of Tangut phonology; in particular initial consonants, rhymes, and tones are compared with the forms reconstructed in previous studies including that of the present author.

tone_statements.citation: 荒川慎太郎 [Arakawa, Shintarō]. 1999. 夏藏対音資料からみた西夏語の声調 [A Study on the Tone of Tangut from Tibetan Transcriptions]. 言語学研究 (Gengogaku Kenkyū / Linguistic Research, Kyoto University Linguistics Circle) 17-18: 27-44.
tone_statements.quote: According to some Tangut phoneticians, it is said that there were two basic tones -平 level tone and 上 raising tone- in Tangut, but descriptions of the value of Tangut tones have not been shown. This study shows that syllables of level tone were transcribed as CCV in Tibetan script because C1- was added to the basic transcription CV, and that syllables of raising tone were transcribed in CV. That is to say, in Tibetan transcription, the syllables of level tone were expressed as high tone and the syllables of raising tone as low tone. Moreover, according to the meanings of the Tangut characters, I have come to the conclusion that level tone was the high-level tone and the raising tone was low-raising tone.
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 (平 level = high-level, 上 rising = low-rising)

tone_statements.quote: Let us consider some particulars of the Tibetan transcriptions. The Tibetan of that period lacked tonal distinctions, and the tones of Tangut are consequently not distinguished in the Tibetan transcriptions. Furthermore, on the basis of the combinations of Tibetan letters in these transcriptions, which are sometimes not only atypical but even utterly alien to conventions of Tibetan orthography, we may conclude that the phonology of the Tibetan of that period differed in a fundamental way from the phonology of Tangut.

tone_statements.translation: Hence one can infer that the opposition between these two classes lay in one being pronounced in the level tone [a low level type] and the other in the level-departing tone [a type falling from level?]. ... tone_statements.citation: 孙伯君 [Sun, Bojun]. n.d. 西夏语声调问题再探 [The question of Tangut tones re-examined]. Listed on the author's publication page, University of Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (teacher.ucass.edu.cn/sunbojun); venue and year not recovered.
tone_statements.quote: 综上,结合《小学问答集》这份音韵材料,我们可以对西夏语声调的性质有如下认识:1)西夏语没有真正意义上的四声,只有平、上两个调类,去声摄于平声。2)西夏语声调是“清平”、“浊上”的格局,对照藏语方言声调高低分化的条件,即清高浊低,可以知道西夏语平声为高调,上声为低调。声调的产生与复辅音的简化和辅音韵尾的脱落息息相关。3)...虽然声调不具有重要的音位价值,即不需要靠它区分大量的词义和语法意义,但还是有一些同声韵的词,需要依靠声调区分词义,且调型并不十分固定,念得高点、低点都不会引起听话人的误解。
tone_statements.translation: In sum, with the phonological material of the Xiaoxue wendaji we can understand the nature of Tangut tone as follows: 1) Tangut had no four tones in the true sense, only two tone categories, ping and shang; qusheng is subsumed under ping. 2) Tangut tone shows a 'voiceless-ping', 'voiced-shang' pattern; by the conditions of the high/low tone split in Tibetan dialects (voiceless high, voiced low) we know the Tangut ping tone was a high tone and the shang tone a low tone. The rise of tone is closely tied to cluster simplification and loss of consonant codas. 3) ...although tone had no great phonemic value, i.e. it was not needed to distinguish large numbers of lexical and grammatical meanings, there were still some words of identical initial and rhyme that relied on tone to distinguish meaning, and the contour was not very fixed: reading it a bit higher or lower would not cause a listener to misunderstand.
tone_statements.summary: Philological reconstruction (extinct language): ping = high, shang = low; p.37 cites Arakawa 1999 (ping high level, shang low rising); low functional load per author; sec. 4 on possible sandhi.

tone.translation: In Tangut phonology [the native Xixia science], rhymes 1-97 are set up in the level tone (平声) and rhymes 1-86 in the rising tone (上声). For example level-tone rhyme 14 and rising-tone rhyme 12 stand in a matching relation (they are rhymes opposed to each other by the difference of tone class). ... The Wenhai is first divided into a main part and the 'zalei'; the main part is divided into volume 1 and volume 2 according to the tone of the listed characters, and the zalei too is divided by the tone of the listed characters into a first half listing level-tone characters and a second half listing non-level-tone characters (typically rising-tone characters). ... The reconstruction in Gong's system is khu² (the superscript number indicates the tone class: 1 = level tone, 2 = rising tone).

sources.quote: According to some Tangut phoneticians, it is said that there were two basic tones -平 level tone and 上 raising tone- in Tangut, but descriptions of the value of Tangut tones have not been shown. This study shows that syllables of level tone were transcribed as CCV in Tibetan script because C1- was added to the basic transcription CV, and that syllables of raising tone were transcribed in CV. That is to say, in Tibetan transcription, the syllables of level tone were expressed as high tone and the syllables of raising tone as low tone. Moreover, according to the meanings of the Tangut characters, I have come to the conclusion that level tone was the high-level tone and the raising tone was low-raising tone.
sources.note: Native Tangut phonologists distinguished two tones (平 level, 上 rising) but their values were undescribed; Tibetan transcriptions write level-tone syllables with a prefixed consonant (CCV) and rising-tone syllables as CV, i.e. level = high, rising = low; concludes level tone = high-level, rising tone = low-rising.

sources.quote: 综上,结合《小学问答集》这份音韵材料,我们可以对西夏语声调的性质有如下认识:1)西夏语没有真正意义上的四声,只有平、上两个调类,去声摄于平声。2)西夏语声调是“清平”、“浊上”的格局,对照藏语方言声调高低分化的条件,即清高浊低,可以知道西夏语平声为高调,上声为低调。声调的产生与复辅音的简化和辅音韵尾的脱落息息相关。3)...虽然声调不具有重要的音位价值,即不需要靠它区分大量的词义和语法意义,但还是有一些同声韵的词,需要依靠声调区分词义,且调型并不十分固定,念得高点、低点都不会引起听话人的误解。

tone.translation: In sum, with the phonological material of the Xiaoxue wendaji we can understand the nature of Tangut tone as follows: 1) Tangut had no four tones in the true sense, only two tone categories, ping and shang; qusheng is subsumed under ping. 2) Tangut tone shows a 'voiceless-ping', 'voiced-shang' pattern; by the conditions of the high/low tone split in Tibetan dialects (voiceless high, voiced low) we know the Tangut ping tone was a high tone and the shang tone a low tone. The rise of tone is closely tied to cluster simplification and loss of consonant codas. 3) ...although tone had no great phonemic value, i.e. it was not needed to distinguish large numbers of lexical and grammatical meanings, there were still some words of identical initial and rhyme that relied on tone to distinguish meaning, and the contour was not very fixed: reading it a bit higher or lower would not cause a listener to misunderstand.
